# Area Under the Dirichlet Function on $[0,1]$

## Identifying the Function

The given function is the **Dirichlet function** (indicator of the irrationals on $[0,1]$):

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \in \mathbb{Q} \\ 1, & x \notin \mathbb{Q} \end{cases}$$

## Step 1: Check Riemann Integrability

For **any** partition $P: 0 = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = 1$ of $[0,1]$, every subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ contains both rational and irrational numbers (by density). Therefore:

$$\sup_{[x_{i-1},x_i]} f = 1, \qquad \inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]} f = 0$$

The upper and lower Darboux sums are:

$$U(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^n 1\cdot(x_i - x_{i-1}) = 1, \qquad L(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^n 0\cdot(x_i - x_{i-1}) = 0$$

Since $U(f,P) - L(f,P) = 1$ for **every** partition, the Riemann integral **does not exist**.

## Step 2: Compute the Lebesgue Integral (the true "area")

The Lebesgue integral handles this function naturally. We use the key fact:

- $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ is **countable**, so its Lebesgue measure is $m(\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]) = 0$.
- The irrationals in $[0,1]$ have measure $m([0,1]) - 0 = 1$.

Since $f$ is measurable (it is the indicator of the measurable set $[0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q}$):

$$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = 0\cdot m(\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]) + 1\cdot m\bigl([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q}\bigr) = 0\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1 = 1$$

Equivalently: $f(x) = 1$ **almost everywhere** on $[0,1]$ (it equals $0$ only on a measure-zero set), so the area equals the area of a $1 \times 1$ rectangle.

## Result

The area under the curve (Lebesgue integral) is:

$$\boxed{1}$$
